plan.paradox: A razor sells itself. And you never buy the handle.
plan.odd_fact: First year sales look absurdly generous.
plan.twist: It locks you into buying blades forever
plan.cause: The razor-only option creates the initial purchase; the blade packs generate recurring sales
plan.everyday: Coffee shop: $5 cup, $2 refill pack, $10 premium brew  -  the refill pack feels cheap and forces repeat buys. Gym: $30 membership, $15 starter kit, $5 class pass  -  the starter kit appears affordable, so you keep paying for classes. The cheap entry wins because it promises future spend.
plan.rule: Watch for a cheap entry that forces future purchases. Follow for more.

beats.say: A razor sells itself. And you never buy the handle.
Buy a razor plus a handful of blades.
Buy a razor with a tiny starter pack.
Buy just the razor, no blades included.
The first-year bundle looks absurdly generous. Looks odd.
In 1903 Gillette sold 51 razors and 168 blades.
In 1904 the tally jumped to 90,884 razors and 123,648 blades.
Every razor sold creates a blade-buyer.
That's roughly three blades for each razor.
The razor is a one-time cost; the blades become the endless revenue stream.
You see it everywhere - a café offers a $5 cup, a $2 refill pack, and a $10 premium brew.
A gym lists a $30 membership, a $15 starter kit, and a $5 class pass.
The cheap starter feels like a deal, so you keep paying for refills or classes.
Watch for a cheap entry that forces future purchases. Follow for more.
